# DISTRIBUTED QUANTUM ALGORITHMS CANNOT COLOR CYCLES WITH PROBABILITY 1

Abstract. We prove that any _distributed quantum algorithm_ that finds a 3-coloring with probability 1 in a cycle of anonymous identical computers has to be global, that is, it needs \(\Omega(n)\) communication rounds. It follows that quantum computation and communication does not help with this problem.

All prior lower bounds on quantum advantage in distributed graph algorithms use arguments related to physical causality. However, it is known that such arguments cannot rule out fast quantum advantage for 3-coloring cycles. In particular, any causality-based argument would rule out the existence of _finitely dependent coloring_, but Holroyd and Liggett (2016) showed that such colorings do exist.

Hence to tackle this problem, we need a "genuinely quantum" lower-bound technique that can distinguish between (1) distributions that do not violate physical causality vs. (2) distributions that can be realized with a quantum strategy. We present the first such lower-bound technique in this context. First, we show that 1-round quantum algorithms cannot break symmetry with probability 1. Second, we present a _wishful teleportation_ strategy that can be used to turn _T_-round quantum 3-coloring algorithms into 1-round quantum algorithms breaking symmetry, while preserving success probability 1. Put together, the lower bound follows.

### 1. Introduction

In this work, we present the first "genuinely quantum" lower bound that puts limits on quantum advantage in distributed symmetry breaking and coloring of cycle. In particular, we show that no distributed quantum algorithm can color cycles with probability 1 in a sublinear number of rounds. Previous lower bounds were established only for _finitely dependent distributions_, a computational model that contains distributed quantum algorithms while remaining easier to analyse. However, finitely dependent colorings of cycles are known to exist [HL16]. Hence, our work is the first inherently quantum lower bound that separates distributed quantum algorithms from finitely dependent distributions.

#### 1.1. Quantum Advantage for Distributed Symmetry Breaking.

One of the biggest open questions related to distributed quantum advantage is whether quantum computation and communication help with distributed symmetry-breaking problems [GKM09; ACdLLMMPRRS25; Suo24; dAm25]. The canonical symmetry-breaking primitive is 3-coloring directed paths and cycles; if this problem can be solved efficiently, all other symmetry-breaking tasks can also be solved efficiently.

The main formalism where this question has been studied is the LOCAL model of distributed computing [Lin92; Pel00]: we have a cycle formed by _n_ computers; they are initially labeled with poly(_n_)-sized unique identifiers; computation proceeds in synchronous rounds; in each round, each node can send a message to each neighbor and update its state based on the messages it receives; and eventually, after some _T_ rounds, each node must stop and announce its own color.

<tbc>In this classical deterministic setting, the complexity of the task is very well-understood since the 1990s: \(\Theta(log^*n)\) communication rounds is sufficient \[CV86; GPS88\] and necessary \[Lin92\]. Even if we allow randomness and only require a correct solution with high probability (w.h.p., with probability 1-1/poly(_n_)), it is known that \(\Theta(log^*n)\) rounds are still necessary \[Nao91\].

But does anything change if we switch from classical LOCAL to the quantum-LOCAL model \[GKM09; AF14\], where each node is a quantum computer and can exchange qubits with its neighbors? While we have seen a lot of progress in understanding which distributed problems admit quantum advantage and which problems remain hard in quantum-LOCAL \[GKM09; AF14; LNR19; DKLMMSS24; ACdLLMMPRRS25; BBCdELLMORSTV25; BCdEKLOSS26; BCCdELMOS25; BG26\], the seemingly elementary question of 3-coloring cycles has remained open, even though essentially the same question was already posed in the very first paper that introduced the quantum-LOCAL model \[GKM09\]. Nobody has been able to rule out the possibility that there is, for example, a quantum-LOCAL algorithm that 3-colors cycles in a constant number _O_(1) of rounds of communication.

## 1.2. Barrier: Finitely Dependent Colorings.

There is a barrier that has so far prevented progress on this question. To our knowledge, all known lower bounds in the quantum-LOCAL model are _indirect_: they do not directly study the quantum-LOCAL model (or any model of quantum computing), but they study strictly stronger models, such as finitely dependent distributions \[BGM93; HL16; ACdLLMMPRRS25\], non-signaling distributions \[GKM09; AF14\], and the online-LOCAL model \[AELMSS23; ACdLLMMPRRS25\]. These lower bounds fundamentally build on the idea that distributed quantum algorithms cannot violate physical causality--information must be carried by communicated systems and correlated event must share a common cause.

Unfortunately, this avenue is blocked for the case of symmetry-breaking problems, and especially for the case of 3-coloring cycles. It is known that there exists a finitely dependent distribution of 3-colorings in cycles \[HL16\]. It follows that a hypothetical constant-round quantum algorithm for 3-coloring cycles would not violate causality, and hence purely causality-based arguments cannot be used.

Therefore, any proof that shows the impossibility of efficient 3-coloring in quantum-LOCAL must be "genuinely quantum", in the sense that it cannot as a byproduct rule out finitely dependent distributions, non-signaling distributions, or online-LOCAL algorithms.

We point out that there is a paper that rules out one-round, one-sided algorithms for 3-coloring \[LR22; GKZ19\] and, very recently, a paper proving that 3-coloring \(\Delta\)-ary trees with \(\Delta\ge 300\) requires \(\Omega(log^*\Delta)\) rounds \[FMZ26\]. Both lower bounds are about the non-signaling model, i.e., causality-based--fundamentally different techniques are needed for stronger lower bounds.

## 1.3. Our Contribution.

In this work, we present the _first "genuinely quantum" lower bound for the task of distributed_ 3_-coloring_; our lower bound _separates quantum algorithms from finitely dependent distributions._ We prove that there is no _o(n_)-round quantum algorithm using finitely many qubits in anonymous cycles that produces a 3-coloring with probability 1; the precise statement is as follows:

**Theorem 1.** _For every fixed_ \(c\ge 3\) _and every even_ \(n\ge 4\)_, any quantum-PN algorithm that properly c-colors directed n-cycles with probability_ 1 _takes_ \(T(n)>\lfloor n/2\rfloor-2\) _rounds._

We note that our result comes with two assumptions:

(1) We work in the quantum-PN model; this is the _anonymous_ version of quantum-LOCAL (with finitely many qubits). In particular the nodes do not have unique identifiers.

(2) We only rule out algorithms that work with _probability_ 1; our result does not rule out algorithms that work w.h.p.

We argue that, while somewhat nonstandard, this setting is still relevant and nontrivial:

(1) While probability-1 classical algorithms do not usually make much sense, there are several examples of nontrivial distributed quantum algorithms that indeed guarantee success with probability 1 using only finitely many qubits; examples include the quantum algorithm for distributed symmetry-breaking in two-node networks \[Gid14\] and the solution strategy for the GHZ game \[GHZ89\].<tbc>

(2) The finitely dependent colorings \[HL16\] are also error-free, and hence a direct distributed analogue would be a quantum algorithm with success probability 1. Moreover, they are invariant under shifts, which would naturally correspond to a quantum algorithm in the anonymous setting.

1 gives an overview of what is now known about the 3-coloring problem across various models of computing.

### 1.4. Open Questions.

After this work, the main open question is extending our result from algorithms that work with probability 1 to algorithms that work w.h.p. We believe that this is the only essential missing part before we can close the long-standing open question. As soon as we look at algorithms that work w.h.p., the distinction between anonymous networks and networks with unique identifiers essentially disappears (since random identifiers will be unique w.h.p.).

**The quantum-PN model (Section 3).** Since nodes are in a cycle, we identify them using integers from 1 to n understood cyclically modulo _n_. In the quantum-PN model, communications rounds are seen as swap gates in a quantum circuit, see Figure 1. Each node manipulates three local registers, local computation steps correspond to unitary matrices, and that the output colors are obtained by a final projective measurement. Using a standard Stinespring dilation, by increasing the dimension of the local registers, one can verify that this model captures the more general definition of quantum-PN in which unitary matrices can be any local quantum transformation (i.e., any CPTP map).

## Round Reduction (Section 6).

We now give an informal overview of the reduction from _T_-round coloring algorithms to one-round symmetry breaking. Suppose that there exists a quantum-PN algorithm A which produces a proper coloring in _T_ communication rounds with probability 1. We show how to transform A into a one-round quantum-PN algorithm B which breaks symmetry on every block of 2_T_+2 consecutive nodes, meaning that such a block can never produce identical outputs. The idea is for B to simulate A using only one communication round. In this single round, neighboring nodes distribute enough maximally entangled states to support all the communication that A would perform during its _T_ rounds. Afterwards, every message that A would send is simulated by teleportation, but without sending the classical teleportation outcome. We call this procedure _wishful teleportation_.

Recall that in standard teleportation \[BBCJPW93\], a node _p_ can transmit a quantum state \(|\psi\rangle\) to a node \(p'\) using a shared maximally entangled state \(|\Phi\rangle\) and classical communication. To do so, _p_ performs a joint measurement on \(|\psi\rangle\) and its share of \(|\Phi\rangle\), obtaining a classical outcome _k_, also known as the _teleportation key_. The system held by \(p'\) then becomes similar to \(|\psi\rangle\), up to some correction _P<sub>k</sub>_. Thus, once _p_ communicates the classical key _k_ to \(p'\), the exact state \(|\psi\rangle\) can be recovered by \(p'\). In wishful teleportation, we replace the communication of _k_ by a guess of translation-invariant keys. This is likely to fail, but our reduction algorithm B can exploit it by outputting the guessed keys together with the outcome of the attempted simulation of A : if every guess is correct, then the simulation algorithm B faithfully reproduces A , which by assumption breaks symmetry; otherwise, the incorrect guess itself breaks symmetry. This guarantees that symmetry is broken by a one-round algorithm B whether A is faithfully simulated or not.

More precisely, in each round of communication \(t\in\{1,2,\dots,T\}\) simulated by wishful teleportation, node _p_ obtains two teleportation keys: _k<sub>t,L</sub>(p_) and _k<sub>t,R</sub>(p_) for the states it respectively attempts to teleport to its neighbors on the left (node _p_-1) and right (node _p_+1). To recover the states sent by nodes _p_-1 and _p_+1, node _p_ would need the keys _k<sub>t,R</sub>(p_-1) and _k<sub>t,L</sub>(p_+1), which are not communicated. Instead, _p_ simply guesses that they satisfy

(3) \(k_{t,R}(p)=k_{t,R}(p-1)\text{and}k_{t,L}(p)=k_{t,L}(p+1),\)

and applies the corrections _P_<sub>_k<sub>t,R</sub>(p_)</sub> and _P_<sub>_k<sub>t,L</sub>(p_)</sub> to the appropriate registers. Whenever these equalities hold, the corresponding teleportation step succeeds. See Figure 2 for an illustration.

<tbc>Repeating this procedure for all \(t\in[T]\) simulated rounds gives each node a list of teleportation keys. After the simulation, each node _p_ performs the final measurement prescribed by A and obtains _a(p_). The output of _p_ in B is then

\(\big(k_{1,L}(p),k_{1,R}(p),\dots,k_{T,L}(p),k_{T,R}(p),a(p)\big).\)

Now consider the output of any block of 2_T_+2 consecutive nodes. If every teleportation guess inside the block is correct, then A is simulated faithfully on its two central nodes, which receive different colors because by assumption \(a(p)\neq a(p+1)\) in A . Otherwise, some teleportation guess is incorrect. This means that at least one condition in Eq (3) fails somewhere inside the block, thus at least one pair of guessed teleportation keys differ between two nodes in that block. Since these keys are included in the output, the outputs on the block cannot all be identical. Hence, B breaks symmetry in a single communication round.

## Finitely many qubits and error probability.

Our analysis of one-round algorithms only rules out the existence of a finite-dimensional quantum algorithm, with local systems of dimension _d_<sup>3</sup>, that solves 3-coloring in _O_(1) rounds with success probability 1. Since the error probability of an algorithm can be written as a polynomial with integer coefficients and real variables, once it is known to be non-zero, results from optimization (see \[JPT13, Theorem 1.1\]) provide a lower bound on the error probability: for each fixed _d_, the success probability is upper bounded by \(1-\varepsilon(d)\), for some \(\varepsilon(d)>0\) that may go to zero as \(d\rightarrow\infty\). Because our argument for the one-round impossibility (Section 5) uses an MPS representation, where the local dimension plays a central role, it is not clear how to obtain a dimension-independent bound \(1-\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon>0\) independent of _d_.

Such a dimension-independent lower bound on the error probability would concern infinite- dimensional quantum strategies as defined by the _tensor-product_ model of quantum theory (see e.g. Def. 1 and Def. 1, 4 of \[LG23\]). This model extends finite-dimensional quantum theory<tbc>

<tbc>by allowing arbitrary Hilbert spaces while preserving the tensor-product rule for combining separated systems.1

There is, however, a more general _commuting-operator_ model of quantum theory, where independent systems are associated to commuting operator algebras acting on a common Hilbert space (see e.g. Def. 2, 3, 5 of \[LG23\]). This model strictly contains the closure of the tensor-product model, as follows from the breakthrough result MIP<sup>∗</sup>=RE \[JNVWY21\].2

For standard bipartite Bell scenarios, the main systematic tool for proving that a distribution is impossible in the commuting-operator model is the Navascués-Pironio-Acín (NPA) hierarchy \[NPA07; NPA08\]. In contrast, the result MIP<sup>∗</sup>=RE implies that there can be no analogous complete decision procedure for the tensor-product model in full generality. Thus, a natural route for extending our lower bound beyond finite-dimensional exact strategies is to reformulate it directly in the commuting-operator model, and to use distributed analogues of the NPA hierarchy, such as the inflation-NPA hierarchy \[WPGRAN21\].

## 3. Preliminaries

### Mathematical Notation.

We use N, R, and C to denote the integers greater than zero, the reals, and the complex numbers respectively. For an integer \(n\ge 1\), we use \[_n_\]={1,2_,...,n_}. For a Hilbert space _H_, we use \(|u\rangle\) to denote vectors of _H_ and \(\langle u|\) for the corresponding co-vector. The space of complex \(d\times d\) matrices is written Mat_<sub>d</sub>_(C) and the space of endomorphisms of a vector space _E_ is denoted by End(_E_). The identity matrix is written as 1. Given an operator _P_, we write the adjoint (i.e., the conjugate-transpose), the conjugate and the transpose as _P_<sup>†</sup>, <o>_P_</o> and \(P^\top\), respectively.

### 3.1. Quantum Information Theory Basics.

We present here the essential for following our proofs and refer readers to \[NC10; Wat18\] for an extensive introduction.

For \(d\in\mathbb{N}\), a _d_-dimensional _register_ is a complex Euclidian space isomorphic to C_<sup>d</sup>_ and represents a physical device holding information. Throughout, we use sans-serif letters X,Y,Z to represents registers. A _state vector_ on X is simply a vector \(u\in\mathsf{X}\). A _(quantum) state_ on register \(\mathsf{X}\simeq\mathbb{C}^d\) is a density matrix \(\rho\): (1) \(\rho\) is a \(d\times d\) matrix with complex coefficients, (2) \(\rho\) is positive semi-definite, and (3) the trace of \(\rho\) is one. To provide some intuition, recall that from the spectral theorem, any positive semi-definite matrix (and, in particular, any density matrix) \(\rho\) can be written as

(4) \(\rho=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|,\)

where the \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_r\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) are the eigenvalues of \(\rho\) and \(|u_1\rangle,|u_2\rangle,\dots,|u_r\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^d\) are the corresponding eigenvectors. Since the trace of \(\rho\) is one, we have that \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\); in other words, \(\rho\) describes a probability distribution over state vectors. When \(\rho=|u\rangle\langle u|\) has rank one, we say that it is a _pure state_. A state on two registers X,Y is a state on \(\mathsf{X}\otimes\mathsf{Y}\).

Operations on a quantum state are in full generality represented by quantum channels. For the purpose of this paper, we only need two kinds of operations on quantum states: applying a unitary, and performing a measurement followed by some classical computation. If X is in a state \(\rho\) and we apply the unitary _U_ on _X_, the state becomes \(U\rho U^\dagger\). For intuition, consider applying _U_ to each \(|u_i\rangle\) in Eq (4) and observe the resulting density matrix. A _measurement_ on

## 3.2. The quantum-LOCAL and quantum-PN models.

The quantum-LOCAL model is a model of distributed quantum computing. The network is represented by a graph where each vertex is a quantum processor, and each edge allows quantum communication between neighboring nodes. Computation proceeds in synchronous rounds. In each round, every node may perform arbitrary local quantum computation and exchange quantum messages of unbounded size with its neighbors. After the last round, each node performs a quantum measurement and outputs a classical string. Thus, quantum-LOCAL is a natural quantum analogue of the classical LOCAL model of distributed algorithms3, obtained by replacing local classical computation and communication with their quantum counterparts.

In LOCAL, hence also in quantum-LOCAL, the nodes are given unique identifiers, usually of _O_(log_n_) bits. When nodes are not provided unique identifiers, the classical model is called the _port-numbering_ model, henceforth PN. Randomized PN algorithms that err with probability at most 1/poly(_n_) can sample random identifiers before the first round, hence randomized PN was heavily used to prove lower bounds in the LOCAL model (e.g., in \[BFHKLRSU16; BBHORS19\]). In this paper, our focus is the _quantum-PN_ model, i.e., the quantum-LOCAL model in which nodes are not provided unique identifiers. As the lower bound from Theorem 1 applies only to zero-error protocols, it does _not_ imply a lower bound in the quantum-LOCAL model.

In this paper, the underlying communication graph is always a _directed cycle_, hence the adjacency relations are implicit in the following definition. Each node has three registers -- left, middle, and right -- to which it can apply a local quantum transformation, and a round of communication swaps the content of the left and right registers between adjacent nodes. To specify an algorithm, it therefore suffices to give a sequence of local quantum transformations and the final measurement.

In full generality, a quantum transformation is described by a Completely Positive Trace Preserving (CPTP) map, see \[Wat18, Eq. 1.124 and 1.125\] for the definition. By Stinespring dilation (\[Wat18, Proposition 2.20\]), any CPTP map can be implemented by a unitary transformation on a larger Hilbert space. Since the local dimension in the quantum-PN model is arbitrary, this enlarged space can be embedded in the model. Thus, quantum-PN algorithms can be defined in terms of unitary transformations without loss of generality. The final measurement is formally described by a POVM as defined in Section 3.1. See Figure 1 for an illustration.

## 4. Proof of Theorem 1

In this section, we formally state our two main technical contributions, Theorems 2 and 3, and use them to prove Theorem 1: any _T(n_)-round quantum-PN algorithm that _c_-colors _n_-cycles with \(T(n)\le n/2-2\) must produce a monochromatic edge with non-zero probability. The choice of the quantum-PN algorithm can depend on _n_, in other words the nodes have knowledge of _n_.

Let us introduce some terminology first. For a quantum-PN algorithm A , the _support_ of A is the set of vectors \(\vec{a}\in\bigcup_{n\ge 3}\Sigma^n\) that A outputs with non-zero probability. For \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), an _r-block_ is a set of _r_ consecutive natural numbers. We say that the _r_-block _B_ is _monochromatic_ in \(\vec{a}=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\Sigma^n\) if and only if all _a<sub>i</sub>_ for \(i\in B\) have the same value. In particular, a coloring algorithm that errs with zero probability is such that all output vectors containing a monochromatic 2-block have probability zero.

First, we prove that any 1-round quantum-PN algorithm produces a monochromatic (_n_-2)- block with non-zero probability, no matter the number of output labels.

**Theorem 2.** _Let_ \(n\ge 4\) _an integer. Any 1-round quantum-PN algorithm has a monochromatic_ (_n_-2)_-block in its support._

Then, we prove that any _T(n_)-round _c_-coloring algorithm can be turned into a 1-round algorithm where nodes output values from \([d]^{4T}\times[c]\) and produces no monochromatic (2_T(n_)+2)- block.

**Theorem 3.** _Let_ \(r\in\mathbb{N}\) _and_ \(n\ge 4\) _and_ \(T\le\lfloor\frac{n-r}{2}\rfloor\)_. ## 6. Round Reduction (Theorem 3)

In this section, we prove our second main technical contribution.

**Theorem 3.** _Let_ \(r\in\mathbb{N}\) _and_ \(n\ge 4\) _and_ \(T\unknown\lfloor\frac{n-r}{2}\rfloor\)_. Suppose there is a T-round quantum- PN algorithm_ \(\mathscr{A}=(U_0,U_1,\dots,U_T,\Pi)\) _of local dimension_ \(d\in\mathbb{N}\) _with outputs in_ \(\Sigma\) _and no monochromatic r-block in its support. Then there exists a 1-round algorithm_ B _with outputs in_ \([d]^{4T}\times\Sigma\) _and no monochromatic_ (2_T+r)-block in its support._

The mechanism behind algorithm B is that each vertex locally instantiates _T_ maximally entangled states with local dimension _d_ for each of its two neighbors, and uses the unique communication round to send the halves of each of those entangled states to the respective neighbor. Each pair of neighbouring vertices thus shares 2_T_ maximally entangled states. Using these states, nodes can attempt to simulate the original _T_-round algorithm A through wishful teleportation (see Figure 2). At the end of B, each vertex outputs the outcome of the attempted simulation of A together with all generated keys used for wishful teleportation.

### 6.1. Background on Teleportation.

Suppose we have a state \(|\psi\rangle_\mathsf{EX}\), where E is an environment register and X is a register held by some node. We wish to turn this state into \(|\psi\rangle_\mathsf{EZ}\) where Z is held by a different node but without using quantum communication. This can be achieved with quantum teleportation \[BBCJPW93\]. Fix the standard maximally entangled vector \(|\Phi\rangle=d^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^d|ii\rangle\) in \(\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d\). Let \(\{P_k:k\in[d^2]\}\) be an orthonormal unitary basis and \(|\Phi_k\rangle=(\mathbb{1}\otimes P_k^\top)|\Phi\rangle\) the associated maximally entangled basis. With these conventions, the teleportation identity is

(7) \(|\psi\rangle_\mathsf{EX}\otimes|\Phi\rangle_\mathsf{YZ}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{k\in[d^2]}|\Phi_k\rangle_\mathsf{XY}\otimes(\mathbb{1}_\mathsf{E}\otimes P_k^\dagger)|\psi\rangle_\mathsf{EZ}.\)

Suppose registers XY are measured in the maximally entangled basis, yielding an outcome \(k\in[d^2]\). Then, by applying the correction _P<sub>k</sub>_ on register Z, we recover the state \(|\psi\rangle_\mathsf{EZ}\), provided _k_ is known to the party holding Z. The explicit environment will be important in our proof, and we emphasize that when the state is teleported, correlations between X and E are preserved between Z and E. This is detailed further in Section A.1.

Now consider the case of a chain of vertices, each holding local registers X(_p_), Y(_p_), Z(_p_) for \(p\in[n]\). Assume each pair of registers Y(_p_) and Z(_p_+1) hold a \(|\Phi\rangle\) state, and that the vertices simultaneously teleport the state in their registers X(_p_) to registers Z(_p_+1), for \(p\in[n-1]\). The next lemma states that the overall effect is a relabelling of the X(1)_..._X(_n_-1) registers to Z(2)_..._Z(_n_). See Section A.2 for a proof.

**Lemma 6.1.** _Consider_ \(n\ge 2\) _vertices in a chain, with each vertex_ \(p\in[n]\) _holding three d- dimensional registers_ X(_p_), Y(_p),_ Z(_p). For each_ \(p\in[n-1]\)_, the registers_ Y(_p_) _and_ Z(_p_+1) _share a maximally entangled state_ \(|\Phi\rangle_{\mathsf{Y}(p)\mathsf{Z}(p+1)}\).

<tbc>_Let_ E _be a finite-dimensional environment and let_ \(\rho\) _be a state on_ \(\mathsf{X}(1)\mathsf{X}(2)\cdots\mathsf{X}(n-1)\mathsf{E}\)_. Suppose that each vertex_ \(p\in[n-1]\) _measures_ X(_p_)Y(_p_) _in the maximally entangled basis, obtains outcome k<sub>p</sub>, and the corresponding correction P<sub>k<sub>p</sub></sub> is applied on_ Z(_p_+1)_. Then the resulting state on_ \(\mathsf{Z}(2)\mathsf{Z}(3)\cdots\mathsf{Z}(n)\mathsf{E}\) _is the reduced state obtained from_ \(\rho\) _by relabelling each_ X(_p_) _as_ Z(_p_+1)_, for_ \(p\in[n-1]\).

## 6.2. The Simulation Algorithm.

We refer to B from Theorem 3 as the simulation algorithm and to A as the original algorithm. Let us now describe the simulation algorithm formally. In Step (I), nodes prepare maximally entangled states in registers T (indexed by the round and direction in which they are used), and they share half of each maximally entangled state with their neighbors during Step (II). Note that Step (II) is the unique communication round of this algorithm. Step (III) implements _T_ rounds of wishful teleportation (see Figure 2 for an illustration). Steps (IV) and (V) perform the final measurement and produce the final output of algorithm B.

**Algorithm B.** One-Round Simulation of a _T_-round algorithm \(\mathcal{A}=(U_0,U_1,\dots,U_T,\Pi)\)

(I) Each vertex _p_ prepares registers \(\mathsf{L}_1(p)\otimes\mathsf{M}(p)\otimes\mathsf{R}_1(p)\) in the state \(U_0|000\rangle\), registers L_<sub>t</sub>(p_), R_<sub>t</sub>(p_) for \(t\in[2,T+1]\) in the state \(|0\rangle\), and the registers<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathsf{T}_{t,L}(p)\otimes\mathsf{T}'_{t,L}(p)\text{and}\mathsf{T}_{t,R}(p)\otimes\mathsf{T}'_{t,R}(p)\)<tbc>

<tbc>in the maximally entangled state \(|\Phi\rangle\) for all \(t\in[T]\).<tbc>

(II) Using _one communication round_, for all _p_ and \(t\in[T]\) swap<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathsf{T}'_{t,L}(p)\leftrightarrow\mathsf{R}_{t+1}(p-1)\text{and}\mathsf{T}'_{t,R}(p)\leftrightarrow\mathsf{L}_{t+1}(p+1).\)<tbc>

(III) For \(t\in[T]\) times and _with no communication_, each vertex _p_:<tbc>

(i) measures \(\mathsf{L}_t(p)\otimes\mathsf{T}_{t,L}(p)\) in the basis \(\{\Phi_k,k\in[d^2]\}\), obtains the outcome \(k_{t,L}(p)\in[d^2]\) and then applies the unitary _P<sub>k<sub>t</sub>,L</sub>(p_) on R<sub>_t_+1</sub>(_p_);<tbc>

(ii) measures \(\mathsf{R}_t(p)\otimes\mathsf{T}_{t,R}(p)\) in the basis \(\{\Phi_k,k\in[d^2]\}\), obtains the outcome \(k_{t,R}(p)\in[d^2]\) and then applies the unitary _P<sub>k<sub>t</sub>,R</sub>(p_) on L<sub>_t_+1</sub>(_p_);<tbc>

(iii) applies the unitary _U<sub>t</sub>_ on \(\mathsf{L}_{t+1}(p)\otimes\mathsf{M}(p)\otimes\mathsf{R}_{t+1}(p)\).<tbc>

(IV) Measure \(\Pi\) on \(\mathsf{L}_{T+1}(p)\otimes\mathsf{M}(p)\otimes\mathsf{R}_{T+1}(p)\) and obtains \(a(p)\in\Sigma\) as the outcome.<tbc>

(V) Vertex _p_ outputs<tbc>

(8) \(\lambda_p=(k_{1,L}(p),k_{1,R}(p),\dots,k_{T,L}(p),k_{T,R}(p),a(p)).\)

Compared to the Definition 3.1 of the quantum-PN model, Algorithm B uses mid-circuit measurements and unitaries with classical control. The well-known _principle of deferred measurement_ states that measurements can always be moved to the end of a quantum circuit, and that classically controlled operations can be substituted by conditional quantum gates \[NC10, Sec. 4.4\]. Therefore, B is still a one-round quantum-PN algorithm on directed cycles, in the same sense as in Definition 3.1.

As proven formally below, the simulation algorithm can be understood as having two behaviours. First, suppose the keys obtained in Step (III) are such that

(9) \(k_{t,L}(p)=k_{t,L}(p+1)\text{and}k_{t,R}(p)=k_{t,R}(p-1)\)

for every \(t\in[T]\). Then, the corrections _P<sub>k<sub>t</sub>,L</sub>(p_) and _P<sub>k<sub>t</sub>,R</sub>(p_) applied by vertex _p_ to the registers R<sub>_t_+1</sub>(_p_) and L<sub>_t_+1</sub>(_p_) lead to successful teleportations. Suppose this holds for all adjacent vertices inside an interval _J<sub>s</sub>_=\[_s,s_+2_T+r_-1\], where \(s\in[n]\) and the interval is understood cyclically. Then B correctly simulates A on the interval \[_s+T,s+T+r_-1\], which is at the center of _J<sub>s</sub>_

<tbc>and has length _r_. Since A by assumption has no monochromatic _r_-block, the _a(p_) part of the outputs of B on this central interval cannot be monochromatic. The second behaviour happens if, for some \(t\in[T]\), Eq (9) fails for some pair of vertices inside _J<sub>s</sub>_. Then two adjacent vertices in _J<sub>s</sub>_ have different wishful teleportation keys. Since these keys are included in the output of B, the interval _J<sub>s</sub>_, which has length 2_T+r_, cannot be monochromatic.

## 6.3. Proof of Theorem 3.

Let \(s\in[n]\) and recall that A is assumed to have no monochromatic _r_-block in its support. Fix an interval<tbc>

\(J_s=[s,s+2T+r-1]\)

<tbc>of 2_T+r_ consecutive vertices where \(T\unknown\lfloor\frac{n-r}{2}\rfloor\), hence the interval does not overlap with itself. We prove that _J<sub>s</sub>_ is monochromatic at the end of B with probability zero: for all output labels

\(\lambda=\underbrace{(\kappa_{1,L},\kappa_{1,R},\dots,\kappa_{T,L},\kappa_{T,R},a)}_\kappa\in([d^2])^{2T}\times\Sigma\)

the probability that \(\lambda_p=\lambda\) for every \(p\in J_s\) is zero (recall that \(\lambda_p\) is the output of nodes _p_ in B, see Eq (8)). A union bound on _s_ then implies that none of the _J<sub>s</sub>_ are monochromatic w.p. one, hence that B has no monochromatic (2_T+r_)-block w.p. one.

For \(0\unknown t\unknown T\), define<tbc>

\(I_s(t)=[s+t,s+2T+r-1-t].\)

<tbc>At each round, _I<sub>s</sub>(t_) shrinks by removing one boundary vertex from each side. In particular, _I<sub>s</sub>_(0)=_J<sub>s</sub>_, and _I<sub>s</sub>(T_) has length _r_.

Let \(C_{\kappa,t}(J_s)\) be the event that, for all \(1\unknown\tau\unknown t\) and all \(p\in I_s(\tau)\),

(10) \(k_{\tau,L}(p)=k_{\tau,L}(p+1)=\kappa_{\tau,L}\text{and}k_{\tau,R}(p)=k_{\tau,R}(p-1)=\kappa_{\tau,R}.\)

Equivalently, in each of the first _t_ rounds, the keys needed to simulate the teleportations into all vertices \(p\in I_s(\tau)\) are equal to the corresponding entries of \(\kappa\). We also set \(C_{\kappa,0}(J_s)\) to be the trivial event.

Suppose that the outputs of the nodes in _J<sub>s</sub>_ are monochromatic, that is, \(\lambda_p=\lambda=(\kappa,a)\) for every \(p\in J_s\). Then each teleportation key in the output of each \(p\in J_s\) is equal to the corresponding component of \(\kappa\). Moreover, for every \(1\unknown\tau\unknown T\) and every \(p\in I_s(\tau)\), we have \(p-1,p,p+1\in I_s(\tau-1)\subseteq J_s\), and thus Eq (10) is satisfied. Therefore, a monochromatic _J<sub>s</sub>_ implies that \(C_{\kappa,T}(J_s)\) occurs for some value of \(\kappa\).

To rule out this monochromatic output in _J<sub>s</sub>_, we will show that after conditioning on \(C_{\kappa,T}(J_s)\), the state of B in _I<sub>s</sub>(T_) is the same as the state of A in this interval. Then, since by assumption A outputs no monochromatic _r_-block, it will follow that B cannot have the monochromatic 2_T+r_ block _J<sub>s</sub>_.

Let \(\rho_t^{(\mathscr{A})}(I)\) be the reduced state of A (see Definition 3.1) on an interval _I_ after _t_ rounds of A , which is obtained by tracing out all registers except<tbc>

\(\otimes_{p\in I}\mathsf{L}(p)\otimes\mathsf{M}(p)\otimes\mathsf{R}(p).\)

<tbc>Similarly, let \(\rho_t^{(\mathscr{B})}(I|C_{\kappa,t}(J_s))\) be the reduced state of B after _t_ simulated rounds, conditioned on \(C_{\kappa,t}(J_s)\), on the registers<tbc>

\(\otimes_{p\in I}\mathsf{L}_{t+1}(p)\otimes\mathsf{M}(p)\otimes\mathsf{R}_{t+1}(p).\)

<tbc>We claim that for every \(0\unknown t\unknown T\),

(11) \(\rho_t^{(\mathscr{B})}(I_s(t)|C_{\kappa,t}(J_s))=\rho_t^{(\mathscr{A})}(I_s(t)).\)

<tbc>The case _t_=0 holds because \(C_{\kappa,0}(J_s)\) is the trivial event and after tracing out the teleportation registers of B, it follows from the definition of Algorithm B that both A and B have the same initial state on the registers being compared.

Then assume Eq (11) holds for some _t\<T_. We will prove it also holds for round _t_+1. Let _I<sub>s</sub>(t_)=\[_u,v_\] and _I<sub>s</sub>(t_+1)=\[_u_+1_,v_-1\]. We first analyse the R registers, which in A are communicated one step clockwise. In B, the corresponding transfers happening into the interval _I<sub>s</sub>(t_+1) are<tbc>

\(\mathsf{R}_{t+1}(p)\longrightarrow\mathsf{L}_{t+2}(p+1),p\in[u,v-2].\)

<tbc>Let us apply Lemma 6.1 to the interval \[_u,v_-1\]. We identify the registers X,Y,Z in Lemma 6.1 with B’s registers as<tbc>

\(\mathsf{X}(p)=\mathsf{R}_{t+1}(p),\mathsf{Y}(p)=\mathsf{T}_{t+1,R}(p),\mathsf{Z}(p)=\mathsf{L}_{t+2}(p).\)

<tbc>Any registers of B not treated explicitly are assumed to be included in the environment E of Lemma 6.1. In B, after the communication round, the register T<sub>_t_+1_,R_</sub>(_p_)=Y(_p_) is maximally entangled with L<sub>_t_+2</sub>(_p_+1)=Z(_p_+1), as required by the lemma for \(p\in[u,v-2]\). On the event \(C_{\kappa,t+1}(J_s)\), we have

\(k_{t+1,R}(p+1)=k_{t+1,R}(p)=\kappa_{t+1,R},\forall p\in[u,v-2].\)

Thus, the unitary _P_<sub>_k_<sub>_t_+1_,R_</sub>(_p_+1)</sub> applied on L<sub>_t_+2</sub>(_p_+1) is the proper teleportation correction operation. Therefore, by Lemma 6.1, the overall effect is a relabelling \(\mathsf{R}_{t+1}(p)\longrightarrow\mathsf{L}_{t+2}(p+1)\) for \(p\in[u,v-2]\). \(\rho_{t+1}^{(\mathscr{B})}(I_s(t+1)|C_{\kappa,t+1}(J_s))=\rho_{t+1}^{(\mathscr{A})}(I_s(t+1)).\)

### A.1. Teleportation.

For completeness and to set the notation for Lemma 6.1, we provide a proof of the quantum teleportation identity (Eq (7)) [BBCJPW93].

**Proposition A.1** (Teleportation)**.** _Let_ \(d\ge 1\)_. Suppose Alice holds two d-dimensional registers_ X, Y_, Bob holds one d-dimensional register_ Z _and let_ E _be some finite dimensional register._

_Suppose that the state of_ \(\mathsf{X}\otimes\mathsf{E}\) _is some pure state u and_ \(\mathsf{Y}\otimes\mathsf{Z}\) _is the maximally entangled pair_ \(|\Phi\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{i=1}^d|ii\rangle.\) _There exists an orthonormal basis_ \(\{|\Phi_k\rangle:k\in[d^2]\}\) _of_ \(\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d\) _and a unitary basis_ \(\{P_k:k\in[d^2]\}\) _of_ Mat_d_(C) _such that_ \(|u\rangle_{\mathsf{X},\mathsf{E}}\otimes|\Phi\rangle_{\mathsf{Y},\mathsf{Z}}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{k\in[d^2]}|\Phi_k\rangle_{\mathsf{X},\mathsf{Y}}\otimes(P_k^\dagger\otimes\mathbb{1}_\mathsf{E})|u\rangle_{\mathsf{Z},\mathsf{E}}.\) _Proof._ Let _X_ and _Z_ be the operators such that for all \(j\in[d]\), \(X|j\rangle=|j+1modd\rangle\text{and}Z|j\rangle=\omega^j|j\rangle\text{where}\omega=exp(2i\pi/d).\) For \(a,b\in[d]\), we define _Wa,b=XaZb_ and \(|\Phi_{a,b}\rangle=(\mathbb{1}\otimes W_{a,b})|\Phi\rangle\). Since \(\langle\Phi_{a,b}|\Phi_{c,d}\rangle=\langle\Phi|\mathbb{1}\otimes W_{a,b}^\dagger W_{c,d}|\Phi\rangle=(1/d)Tr(W_{a,b}^\dagger W_{c,d})=\delta_{a,c}\delta_{b,d},\) the \(|\Phi_{a,b}\rangle\) are an orthonormal basis of \(\mathbb{C}^d\otimes\mathbb{C}^d\). Let us now compute the coefficient of \(|v\rangle\otimes|\Phi\rangle\) in the basis \(\{|\Phi_{a,b}\rangle\otimes|c\rangle:a,b,c\in[d]\}\) for some state \(|v\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^d\). Fix \(a,b\in[d]\), then \(\langle\Phi_{a,b}\otimes\mathbb{1}|v\otimes\Phi\rangle=\langle\Phi\otimes\mathbb{1}|\mathbb{1}\otimes W_{a,b}^\dagger\otimes\mathbb{1}|v\otimes\Phi\rangle=\langle\Phi\otimes\mathbb{1}|v\otimes(W_{a,b}^\dagger\otimes\mathbb{1})\Phi\rangle\) Using that \(M\otimes\mathbb{1}|\Phi\rangle=\mathbb{1}\otimes M^\top|\Phi\rangle\) for all \(M\in\mathrm{Mat}_d(\mathbb{C})\) and that \((W_{a,b}^\dagger)^\top=\overline{W_{a,b}}\), we can rewrite \(\langle\Phi_{a,b}\otimes\mathbb{1}|v\otimes\Phi\rangle=\langle\Phi\otimes\mathbb{1}|\mathbb{1}\otimes\mathbb{1}\otimes\overline{W_{a,b}}|v\otimes\Phi\rangle=\overline{W_{a,b}}\langle\Phi\otimes\mathbb{1}|v\otimes\Phi\rangle=(1/d)\overline{W_{a,b}}|v\rangle_\mathsf{Z}\) where we use that _W_a,b acts only on Z here. Hence, we have that (12) \(|v\rangle_\mathsf{X}\otimes|\Phi\rangle_\mathsf{YZ}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{a,b\in[d]}|\Phi_{a,b}\rangle_{\mathsf{X},\mathsf{Y}}\otimes\overline{W_{a,b}}|v\rangle_\mathsf{Z}.\) Consider now the Schmidt decomposition of \(|u\rangle\) in \(\mathsf{X}\otimes\mathsf{E}\), \(|u\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^r|v_i\rangle_\mathsf{X}\otimes|w_i\rangle_\mathsf{E}.\) Applying Eq (12) for each _vi_ and using linearity, \(|u\rangle_{\mathsf{X},\mathsf{E}}\otimes|\Phi\rangle_{\mathsf{Y},\mathsf{Z}}=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{a,b\in[d]}|\Phi_{a,b}\rangle_{\mathsf{X},\mathsf{Y}}\otimes\overline{W_{a,b}}|v_i\rangle_\mathsf{Z}\otimes|w_i\rangle_\mathsf{E}\)
\(=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{a,b\in[d]}|\Phi_{a,b}\rangle_{\mathsf{X},\mathsf{Y}}\otimes(\overline{W_{a,b}}\otimes\mathbb{1}_\mathsf{E})\big(\sum_{i=1}^r|v_i\rangle_\mathsf{Z}\otimes|w_i\rangle_\mathsf{E}\big)\)
\(=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{a,b\in[d]}|\Phi_{a,b}\rangle_{\mathsf{X},\mathsf{Y}}\otimes(\overline{W_{a,b}}\otimes\mathbb{1}_\mathsf{E})|u\rangle_{\mathsf{Z},\mathsf{E}}.\) And thus if one measures \(\mathsf{X}\otimes\mathsf{Y}\) in the basis \(\{|\Phi_{a,b}\rangle\}\) and obtains some outcome _k_=(_a,b_), after applying \(\overline{W_{a,b}^\dagger}\) to Z, we obtain the state \(|u\rangle_{\mathsf{Z},\mathsf{E}}\) which is the same as relabeling X as Z. To recover the notation in the statement, use \(P_k:=W_{a,b}^\top\).

## A.2. Chain teleportation.

Here we prove Lemma 6.1, which states that if teleportation is performed in parallel in a chain of nodes, the overall effect is a relabelling of the registers (see Figure 3).

**Lemma 6.1.** _Consider_ \(n\ge 2\) _vertices in a chain, with each vertex_ \(p\in[n]\) _holding three d- dimensional registers_ X(_p),_ Y(_p),_ Z(_p). For each_ \(p\in[n-1]\)_, the registers_ Y(_p_) _and_ Z(_p_+1) _share a maximally entangled state_ \(|\Phi\rangle_{\mathsf{Y}(p)\mathsf{Z}(p+1)}\).

_Let_ E _be a finite-dimensional environment and let_ \(\rho\) _be a state on_ \(\mathsf{X}(1)\mathsf{X}(2)\cdots\mathsf{X}(n-1)\mathsf{E}\)_. Suppose that each vertex_ \(p\in[n-1]\) _measures_ X(_p_)Y(_p_) _in the maximally entangled basis, obtains outcome k<sub>p</sub>, and the corresponding correction P<sub>k<sub>p</sub></sub> is applied on_ Z(_p_+1)_. Then the resulting state on_ \(\mathsf{Z}(2)\mathsf{Z}(3)\cdots\mathsf{Z}(n)\mathsf{E}\) _is the reduced state obtained from_ \(\rho\) _by relabelling each_ X(_p_) _as_ Z(_p_+1)_, for_ \(p\in[n-1]\).

_Proof._ Let the initial state be

\(\sigma=\rho_{\mathsf{X}(1)\mathsf{X}(2)\cdots\mathsf{X}(n-1)\mathsf{E}}\otimes\otimes_{p=1}^{n-1}|\Phi\rangle\langle\Phi|_{\mathsf{Y}(p)\mathsf{Z}(p+1)},\)

where we consider Z(1),X(_n),_Y(_n_) as part of the environment register E.

Decompose \(\rho\) as

\(\rho=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|_{\mathsf{X}(1)\mathsf{X}(2)\cdots\mathsf{X}(n-1)\mathsf{E}}\)

(cf. Eq (4)), where \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) and \(|u_1\rangle,\dots,|u_r\rangle\in\mathsf{X}(1)\mathsf{X}(2)\cdots\mathsf{X}(n-1)\mathsf{E}\). Let us apply the teleportation identity (Eq (7)) to the X(1)Y(1)Z(2) registers of \(\sigma\). This yields

\(\sigma=\frac{1}{d^2}\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i\sum_{k,\ell\in[d]^2}|\Phi_k\rangle\langle\Phi_\ell|_{\mathsf{X}(1)\mathsf{Y}(1)}\otimes(\overline{P_k}\otimes\mathbb{1})|u_i^{(1)}\rangle\langle u_i^{(1)}|(\overline{P_\ell}\otimes\mathbb{1})^\dagger\otimes\otimes_{p=2}^{n-1}|\Phi\rangle\langle\Phi|_{\mathsf{Y}(p)\mathsf{Z}(p+1)},\)

where \(|u_i^{(1)}\rangle:=|u_i^{(1)}\rangle_{\mathsf{Z}(2)\mathsf{X}(2)\mathsf{X}(3)\dots\mathsf{X}(n-1)\mathsf{E}}\) is obtained from |_u<sub>i</sub>_〉 by relabelling X(1) to Z(2), the unitary <o>_P_</o><sub>k</sub> acts on Z(2), and the identity on \(\mathsf{X}(2)\mathsf{X}(3)\cdots\mathsf{X}(n-1)\mathsf{E}\).
